title: RISC-V For AI: Breakthrough Or Bad Idea?
gist: Experts-at-the-table debate on RISC-V in AI chips: Quadric argues starting an AI accelerator from RISC-V creates a costly CPU/accelerator partition and favors matrix-native designs, while Breker sees RISC-V winning as the custom-instruction control processor replacing accelerator state machines; Siemens EDA and SignatureIP stress trace/observability and system-level NoC verification to catch coherency deadlocks.

themes.theme: Quadric's case against RISC-V-based AI accelerators

insights.claim: Quadric CMO Steve Roddy argues that building an AI accelerator starting from RISC-V is 'a flat-out bad idea' because it forces a partition between a programmable CPU and external accelerator blocks, creating a data-movement problem that needs fancy compilers to fix.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Challenges the bull case for RISC-V as the core of AI inference silicon; favors matrix-native architectures.
insights.quote: We think that starting with RISC-V to do an AI accelerator is a flat-out bad idea, because you instantly create a problem.
insights.locator: Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view

insights.claim: According to Quadric's Roddy, the CPU-accelerator partitioning problem scales badly: the bigger the accelerator (e.g., a 100 TOPS design with 16 RISC-V processors slaved to accelerator blocks), the worse the interconnect, compiler and verification burden becomes.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Scaling partitioned AI chips raises interconnect/verification costs, a structural tax on CPU+accelerator designs.
insights.quote: That’s a problem that scales badly. The bigger the accelerator, the worse it gets.
insights.locator: Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view

insights.claim: Roddy contends that CPU hardware is designed for pointer-chasing and unpredictable multi-thread scheduling, whereas AI inference is known millions of cycles in advance, so most CPU hardware is unnecessary for inference.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Explains why deterministic inference workloads favor statically scheduled, non-CPU architectures.
insights.quote: You know for millions of cycles in advance what’s happening. You don’t need most of the CPU hardware.
insights.locator: Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view

insights.claim: Roddy says DSPs are closer to AI needs but are vector machines, while most of the challenge in AI is matrix-by-matrix, which is why Quadric built a matrix-native machine; he claims the only other close equivalent is Google's data-center TPUs.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Positions Quadric and Google TPU as the only matrix-native designs, implying competitors bear partitioning costs.
insights.quote: And most of what is challenging in AI is matrix-by-matrix. So we built a matrix-native machine.
insights.locator: Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view

insights.claim: Roddy claims that nearly everyone other than matrix-native designs has a partitioned architecture and spends billions of dollars trying to compensate for that starting point.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Suggests large R&D/compiler spend across the AI chip industry is remediation of an architectural choice.
insights.quote: Literally, everybody else has a partitioned problem, and then they struggle and spend billions of dollars trying to handle that partitioning problem
insights.locator: Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view

insights.claim: Breker CEO Dave Kelf reports that in four instances, at both big and small companies, the complex state machines traditionally used to control large AI accelerators (SIMD/SIMT) proved 'hopeless,' so teams replaced them with RISC-V processors as the control function.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Signals a concrete design-win pattern for RISC-V cores as AI accelerator controllers.
insights.quote: What we’ve seen in four instances now, both big and small companies, is that the state machines are hopeless.
insights.locator: Kelf: I agree with Steve’s point

insights.claim: Kelf says teams are adding custom RISC-V instructions for very efficient load/store to cut latency between partitions, plus vector and new matrix-multiplication instructions, while still using a regular compiler.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Custom-instruction extensibility is the concrete feature driving RISC-V adoption in AI control roles.
insights.quote: They’re also putting in their own instructions for very efficient load/store to reduce the latency that you see between partitions.
insights.locator: Kelf: I agree with Steve’s point

insights.claim: Kelf argues Arm and others have built instructions into their processors but these are not variable, making RISC-V uniquely suited to powerful custom instructions; Roddy similarly says the market leader does not allow that level of flexibility for control and CPU functions.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Identifies a durable competitive wedge for RISC-V versus Arm in customizable control cores.
insights.quote: Then, of course, there are people like Arm and others who have built instructions into some of their processors, but they’re not variable.
insights.locator: Kelf: I agree with Steve’s point

insights.claim: Roddy concedes RISC-V CPUs can handle thousands of non-inference tasks more flexibly, efficiently and at a lower price point than fixed-function CPUs from other vendors, but not heavy-lifting inference.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Bounds the RISC-V AI opportunity to control/orchestration rather than compute TAM.
insights.quote: We just don’t think doing heavy lifting and inferencing is the right way to deploy that kind of technology.
insights.locator: Roddy: I spent 17 years at Tensilica

insights.claim: Kelf describes a customer with a SIMT array using a RISC-V control processor to handle math from divergent parallel lanes while the accelerator does the rest; it took a lot of work but is now seen as quite successful.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Shows RISC-V's niche role in handling irregular work alongside accelerators, at significant engineering cost.
insights.quote: They’re not doing heavyweight processing inside the RISC-V. They’re just doing enough to keep the whole machine working and reduce that latency

insights.claim: Kelf notes RISC-V's standardization lets companies get a compiler and potentially move to a different vendor while embedding proprietary extensions, which fixed proprietary processors do not offer.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Vendor portability reduces lock-in risk, an adoption driver that pressures incumbent CPU IP pricing.

insights.claim: Roddy, who spent 17 years at Tensilica, says Tensilica long ago automated custom-instruction generation with matching compilers, simulators and verification, but at the cost of a royalty, while RISC-V offers a way to avoid paying a 'tax to the big guy.'
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Frames RISC-V adoption as royalty avoidance traded against manual engineering effort.
insights.quote: RISC-V is an opportunity to not pay a royalty, a tribute, a tax to the big guy.
insights.locator: Roddy: I spent 17 years at Tensilica

insights.claim: Roddy argues RISC-V only pays off if a team customizes heavily, because for light customization an automated commercial flow like Tensilica's is cheaper than manually building compilers and verification.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Implies RISC-V's ROI is concentrated in deep-customization programs; light users may stay with licensed IP.
insights.quote: if you really want to use RISC-V, you better be going all out and customizing the hell out of it
insights.locator: Roddy: I spent 17 years at Tensilica

themes.theme: Verification, trace and observability for custom AI chips

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Francisca Tan says Tessent supports custom-instruction tracing, letting RISC-V users choose which custom instructions to trace at runtime, and that Siemens donated the Efficient Trace (E-Trace) compressed instruction-trace specification to RISC-V.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Debug/observability tooling is an EDA revenue layer that grows with custom RISC-V adoption.
insights.locator: Tan: In terms of what testing

insights.claim: Tan argues hardware observability (embedded analytics to monitor internal signals and performance during debug and silicon bring-up) is becoming essential as chip complexity rises, extending to interconnect and bus monitoring across the SoC.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Supports demand for in-silicon monitoring IP and embedded analytics.

insights.claim: SignatureIP's Ewald Liess warns that multi-core RISC-V/accelerator systems immediately face cache-coherency problems, and coherency corner cases plus traffic bursts can deadlock the fabric, so NoC verification must happen at the system level.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: System-level interconnect verification is a growing bottleneck and tooling opportunity for multi-core AI SoCs.
insights.quote: The coherency corner cases and traffic bursts can easily cause deadlocks in the fabric.
insights.locator: Leiss: We’ve talked a lot about

insights.claim: Liess notes an instruction can execute correctly yet the chip still fails if the data burst needed for the calculation is not available, meaning ISA-level verification is insufficient.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Highlights a hidden tape-out risk for custom AI chips that ISA compliance does not catch.
insights.quote: an instruction can execute correctly, but the chip can still fail if the data burst needed for the instruction or the calculation isn’t available.
insights.locator: Leiss: We’ve talked a lot about

insights.claim: SignatureIP says customers customize RISC-V cores but stick to standard interfaces (AMBA, CXL, PCI Express, CHI) to reach memory and off-chip resources, so SignatureIP configures its pre-verified NoC rather than the cores.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Standard interfaces anchor NoC IP value even as core designs fragment.
